title: washing before prayer
hook: washing before prayer; water as a reset

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last lines of al-Fatiha, and a prayer that asks for directions. Your line was show me the way. Did you ask anyone for directions? Day nine.

You come home after a long day. Before you do anything else, you go to the sink and run cold water over your hands, and then, without really deciding to, over your face. Something shifts. The day is still the day, but it isn't stuck to you in quite the same way. Most people know that feeling. Muslims have built it into every day, five times over. Before each prayer, there's water first. The hands, the mouth, the face, the arms, the feet. A mosque courtyard often has a row of taps and low stools just for this. Today: the washing that comes before the words.
screen: `COLD WATER AT THE SINK.` → `THE DAY LOOSENS.` → `WATER BEFORE THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: The word is wudu. Its root, w-d-a, carries the sense of brightness and clean light: the same root gives words for a shining face. The Qur'an sets it out in one verse, in Pickthall's words: “When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows.” Then the head is lightly wiped, and the feet. That's the core. Over time the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ showed his companions the whole shape, and it's the shape Muslims use today. It begins with an intention, often with bismillah. Then the hands, three times. Water in the mouth, and the nose. The face, from hairline to chin, ear to ear. Each arm to the elbow. A wet hand over the head, and the ears. The feet. Here Muslims differ, and both sides read the same verse. Sunni Muslims wash the feet. Shia Muslims wipe them with a wet hand. What's it for? A hadith in Muslim's collection pictures it this way: as the water runs off the face, the wrongs the eyes have looked at run off with it; off the hands, what the hands did; off the feet, where the feet went. Another says cleanliness is half of faith. So wudu isn't only hygiene. It's a reset, done with the body, before you speak to God. And if there's no water, in a desert, or when water would harm you, the same verse allows tayammum: touching clean earth and wiping the face and hands. The reset is never out of reach. The day doesn't have to come with you into the prayer.
screen: `WUDU — FROM A ROOT OF BRIGHTNESS.` · `HANDS, MOUTH, FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` · `THE WRONGS RUN OFF WITH THE WATER.` · `NO WATER? CLEAN EARTH.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FACES.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. If there's water nearby, go and wash your hands slowly, and feel it run off your fingers. If there isn't, rest your hands open on your knees and picture cool water running over them, then your face. Either way, choose one thing from today you'd like to rinse off. A sharp word, a worry, a scroll you regret. Let the water take it. The bell holds the time.
Wudu. The washing before prayer: hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet. A reset with water. Ninth word.
Your line: rinse the day off. Tonight, when you wash your face, do it slowly, and let one thing from today go down the drain with the water. Day nine.

howItsDone: Muslims make wudu before each prayer unless they are still in a state of wudu from an earlier washing; mosques have washing areas with taps, and at home it's done at an ordinary sink.

original.note: Arabic: the washing before prayer, from a root of brightness and cleanness.

trapdoor: what you thought: washing your hands before praying, like manners.
what it means: wudu — a set washing of hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet that turns the body toward prayer.
what a scholar hears: a root of brightness; a single verse (5:6) read two ways on the feet, washed by Sunnis and wiped by Shia; and tayammum, so the reset needs only clean earth.

notes: Pickthall 5:6 opening quoted from memory: 'O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles.' Please confirm.
Root of wudu: w-d-' (wada'a, brightness, cleanness). Confirm the root's sense as stated.

The order given is the common Sunni order including sunnah acts (hands, mouth, nose, three times, ears); Shia wudu differs in more than the feet (e.g. direction of washing the arms, and wiping rather than washing). The script names only the feet. Confirm this is enough.
Hadith numbers Muslim 244 and 223 cited from memory; please confirm.
Wudu is not repeated when one is still in a state of purity; howItsDone says so. Confirm phrasing.
